evidence_quotes.quote: Therefore, this research aims to propose and evaluate the Regulatory Index of Quality of Water Supply Service (RIQS) to triage on-site inspections of water supply systems in cities of the state of Minas Gerais.

The objective of this step was to preliminarily select the operational indicators to compose the index. This process focused on the operational information due to the aim of RIQS: prioritizing on-site inspections of water supply systems.

We received contributions from 14 specialists—5 managers and 9 analysts (the same group was consulted in later steps). At the end of this stage, the indicators that comprised each typological group were determined.

Furthermore, we noticed that a municipality could have an excellent grade and be deficient in actions aimed at rural sanitation and at reducing inequality in access to water supply services—despite being extremely relevant, these factors were not directly considered in the RIQS.

By considering the list of supervised municipalities available by Arsae (2022) and the average scores of the supervised and unsupervised municipalities, there is a tiny difference: inspected cities reached an average of 83.8 points in the RIQS, and non-supervised municipalities averaged 85.3 spots.

criterion_notes.c1: The paper designs and evaluates a municipal-level composite operational benchmarking index (RIQS) to help a water regulator prioritize on-site technical inspections of water supply utilities. Although 3 of the 12 sub-indicators relate to concession-area water supply availability/coverage (INA-01, weight 17.2%), distribution outages over 12 hours (INA-04, weight 6.2%), and timely connection requests (INA-11, weight 2.4%), the authors rejected the actual customer connection indicator (index of water supply service) and explicitly state (p. 12) that rural sanitation and inequalities in access to water supply services were not directly considered in RIQS. Service access is not examined separately from overall utility operational quality.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study examines a regulatory factor because it develops a regulatory agency indicator tool (Arsae-MG), elicits AHP weights from 14 Arsae-MG regulatory specialists, and compares composite RIQS scores between Arsae-MG-inspected (supervised) and non-inspected municipalities (plain C2 = yes). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, c2 = no: constructing a multicriteria (AHP) operational index to triage on-site utility inspections is a regulatory management/benchmarking methodology rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement of access/disconnection rules, or utility ownership/regulatory structure directly governing service access), and the brief comparison of general operational utility audits does not evaluate a rule-type mechanism governing access. Even under the plain Criterion 2 reading, the overall full-text decision remains exclude (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because the study fails C1, C4, and C5 by only evaluating a conflated composite operational/water-quality/efficiency index rather than an identifiable service-access outcome.
criterion_notes.c3: Contains primary empirical data and quantitative methods: a two-round adapted Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) survey of 14 Arsae-MG specialists and cross-sectional quantitative analysis of 2020 Arsae-MG operational indicator data across 591 regulated municipalities in Minas Gerais, including descriptive statistics and a Kruskal-Wallis comparison.
criterion_notes.c4: In all municipal-level evaluations and in the sole comparative test (inspected vs. non-inspected municipalities, p. 13), the only reported outcome is the aggregated composite RIQS score (0–100), in which over 74% of the weight reflects drinking-water sampling frequency and potability compliance (28.8%), technical operational efficiency—hydrometer metering, treatment plant hydraulic overload, electricity consumption growth, and water loss per connection (31.9%), leak repair timeliness (5.2%), complaints (6.2%), and connection-inspection deadlines (2.1%), while concession-area coverage (17.2%) already has a 1st quartile of 99.90% and median of 100.00% (Table 4). Disaggregated access, connection, continuity, quantity, or affordability outcomes are never reported or analyzed in relation to any regulatory factor.
criterion_notes.c5: Although the municipal unit of analysis (591 regulated municipalities in Minas Gerais in 2020) and cross-sectional index-construction/validation design are identifiable, an eligible exposure-to-access-outcome relationship cannot be identified: Table 4 reports univariate state-wide quartiles without any exposure variable, Tables 6–7 report expert preference weights, and the inspected vs. non-inspected validation test only reports the conflated composite RIQS score.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English, an eligible language without translation.

study_design: Cross-sectional multicriteria index development and validation study (adapted Analytic Hierarchy Process expert survey and cross-sectional municipal indicator analysis)
population_and_sample: 14 water regulation specialists (5 managers and 9 analysts) at Arsae-MG for AHP indicator weighting, and 591 regulated municipalities in the state of Minas Gerais, Brazil (2020 Arsae-MG operational database; unit of analysis: municipality)
exposure: Regulatory on-site operational inspection supervision status by Arsae-MG (supervised/inspected vs. non-supervised municipalities) in the validation test; no exposure variable for indicator-level descriptive statistics
outcome: Composite Regulatory Index of Quality of Water Supply Service (RIQS, 0–100 scale aggregating 12 effectiveness, efficiency, and customer-relationship indicators) and expert AHP indicator weights; no disaggregated service-access outcome analyzed by regulatory exposure
rationale: Excluded (E04 - Wrong outcome; also fails narrow Criterion 2). This study develops an Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP) composite operational index (RIQS) to help the Minas Gerais water regulator (Arsae-MG) prioritize on-site operational inspections of municipal water utilities. Although concession-area water coverage (INA-01), >12h outages (INA-04), and connection-request timeliness (INA-11) are three of twelve sub-indicators in RIQS, actual household connections were rejected in indicator screening, inequalities in water access and rural sanitation were explicitly not considered (p. 12), and the only outcome evaluated across municipalities (including between previously inspected and non-inspected municipalities, p. 13) is the aggregated composite RIQS score—dominated by potability/sampling, metering, treatment plant overload, electricity consumption, water losses, and leak repairs—with no disaggregated service-access outcome reported by any legal or regulatory exposure. Under narrow Criterion 2, proposing an AHP operational inspection-triage index is also a regulatory benchmarking tool rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access; even under plain Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because no identifiable access outcome is analyzed.
